claim: Triangular current ramps emulate the depolarizing input received by a place cell during a place field traversal.
source: Previously, we found that when triangular shaped current ramps intended to emulate the depolarizing input received by a place cell during a place field traversal (Epsztein et al., 2011) were injected at the soma or dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons, they elicited fewer spikes on the down-ramp than on the up-ramp (Upchurch et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Epsztein et al., 2011 and the authors' previous work (Upchurch et al., 2022).

claim: Triangular current ramps injected at the soma or dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons elicit fewer spikes on the down-ramp than on the up-ramp.
source: Previously, we found that when triangular shaped current ramps intended to emulate the depolarizing input received by a place cell during a place field traversal (Epsztein et al., 2011) were injected at the soma or dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons, they elicited fewer spikes on the down-ramp than on the up-ramp (Upchurch et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Upchurch et al., 2022).

claim: Fewer spikes on the down-ramp compared to the up-ramp is due to adaptation mediated by long-term sodium channel inactivation.
source: Regardless of whether these ramps are injected at the soma or in the dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons, they elicit fewer spikes on the down-ramp than on the up-ramp, due to adaptation mediated by long-term sodium channel inactivation (Fernandez and White, 2010; Venkatesan et al., 2014; Upchurch et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fernandez and White, 2010; Venkatesan et al., 2014; and Upchurch et al., 2022.

claim: Place cell firing is modulated by experience such that the center of mass of the place field shifts in a direction opposite the direction of motion as the environment becomes more familiar.
source: Place cell firing is modulated by experience such that the center of mass of the place field shifts in a direction opposite the direction of motion as the environment becomes more familiar (Mehta et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mehta et al., 2000.

claim: The modulation of place cell firing is strongest when animals are first introduced to a novel environment.
source: This modulation is strongest when animals are first introduced to a novel environment (Roth et al., 2012), suggesting involvement of a novelty signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Roth et al., 2012.

claim: Elevated acetylcholine is a novelty signal.
source: This modulation is strongest when animals are first introduced to a novel environment (Roth et al., 2012), suggesting involvement of a novelty signal. Since elevated acetylcholine is thought to be such a signal (Acquas et al., 1996; Giovannini et al., 2001), we investigated the effect of cholinergic neuromodulation on this firing rate adaptation (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Acquas et al., 1996 and Giovannini et al., 2001.

claim: Application of carbachol (CCh) caused a depolarization of 2–6 mV.
source: Application of the cholinergic agonist carbachol (CCh, 2 µM) caused a depolarization of 2–6 mV.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations reported in the manuscript.

claim: The amplitude of background fluctuations in the resting membrane potential increased from a few tenths of a mV in control to 2–4 mV in CCh.
source: The amplitude of background fluctuations in the resting membrane potential increased from a few tenths of a mV in control to 2–4 mV in CCh.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations reported in the manuscript.

claim: The threshold for action potential generation became more hyperpolarized in the presence of CCh.
source: Moreover, the threshold for action potential generation became more hyperpolarized.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations reported in the manuscript.

claim: CCh caused a shift of the center of mass of firing to later in the ramp.
source: Under these conditions, CCh caused a shift of the center of mass of firing to later in the ramp (Figure 1B1 and 1F1), which resulted in a decreased value of the adaptation index which became negative for most cells, as shown in the scatter plot of group data (Figure 1D and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The shift in center of mass of firing was significant for short (2 s) ramps in the soma (control 0.33±0.02, CCh –0.25±0.03; t(20) = 16.741; p<0.0005; n=21).
source: This shift was significant for short (2 s) ramps in the soma (control 0.33±0.02, CCh –0.25±0.03; t(20) = 16.741; p<0.0005; n=21)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The shift in center of mass of firing was significant for long (10 s) ramps in the soma (control 0.24±0.02, CCh –0.33±0.06; t(18) = 9.854; p<0.0005; n=19).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The shift in center of mass of firing was significant for short (2 s) ramps in the dendrites (control 0.49±0.04, CCh –0.45±0.07; t(18) = 12.529; p<0.0005; n=19).
source: as well as for short and long ramps in the dendrites (2 s ramps: control 0.49±0.04, CCh –0.45±0.07; t(18) = 12.529; p<0.0005; n=19
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The shift in center of mass of firing was significant for long (10 s) ramps in the dendrites (control 0.37±0.02, CCh –0.16±0.06; t(9) = 10.582; p<0.0005; n=10).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Acetylcholine shifted the center of mass of firing to later in the ramp in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Like carbachol, acetylcholine shifted the center of mass of firing to later in the ramp, albeit to a more moderate degree (Figure 3A–D). A one-way repeated measures ANOVA was carried out to determine if there was an effect on the adaptation index of three concentrations of ACh within the same neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was a significant effect of ACh on the adaptation index (control 0.35±0.04; 2 μM ACh 0.14±0.04; 10 μM ACh 0.00±0.06; 15 μM ACh –0.02±0.06; F(1.722, 20.665)=44.360; p<0.0005, n=13).
source: There was a significant effect of ACh on the adaptation index, plotted in Figure 3E (control 0.35±0.04; 2 μM ACh 0.14±0.04; 10 μM ACh 0.00±0.06; 15 μM ACh –0.02±0.06; F(1.722, 20.665)=44.360; p<0.0005, n=13).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Flufenamic acid (FFA) reversed the effect of CCh on the adaptation index in somatic recordings (control 0.35±0.05, CCh –0.36±0.09, CCh + FFA 0.25±0.06; F(2,16) = 65.835; p<0.0005; n=9).
source: The differences in adaptation index across the three conditions were found to be significantly different by repeated measures ANOVA in both somatic recordings (control 0.35±0.05, CCh –0.36±0.09, CCh + FFA 0.25±0.06; F(2,16) = 65.835; p<0.0005; n=9; Figure 4A4)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Flufenamic acid (FFA) reversed the effect of CCh on the adaptation index in dendritic recordings (control 0.52±0.02, CCh –0.54±0.11, CCh + FFA 0.20±0.08; F(2,16) = 60.680; p<0.0005; n=9).
source: and dendritic recordings (control 0.52±0.02, CCh –0.54±0.11, CCh + FFA 0.20±0.08; F(2,16) = 60.680; p<0.0005; n=9; Figure 4B4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The shift in the center of mass of firing to later along the ramp that is associated with cholinergic activity is due, in large part, to activation of TRP channels.
source: Overall, these data suggest that the shift in the center of mass of firing to later along the ramp that is associated with cholinergic activity is due, in large part, to activation of TRP channels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results with FFA.

claim: SKF96365 did not significantly shift the adaptation index in the same manner as FFA.
source: Thus, SKF96365 did not significantly shift the adaptation index in the same manner as did FFA, suggesting that the TRP channels involved in the CCh-mediated forward shift are not of the TRPC subtype.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference between CCh and CCh + SKF conditions.

claim: The TRP channels involved in the CCh-mediated forward shift are not of the TRPC subtype.
source: Thus, SKF96365 did not significantly shift the adaptation index in the same manner as did FFA, suggesting that the TRP channels involved in the CCh-mediated forward shift are not of the TRPC subtype.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results with SKF96365.

claim: CBA reversed the effect of CCh on the adaptation index in somatic recordings (control 0.29±0.05, CCh –0.37±0.10, CCh + CBA 0.17±0.07; F(2,16) = 66.257; p<0.0005; n=9).
source: Repeated measures ANOVA showed significant differences in the adaptation indices in somatic recordings (control 0.29±0.05, CCh –0.37±0.10, CCh + CBA 0.17±0.07; F(2,16) = 66.257; p<0.0005; n=9; Figure 5A4)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: CBA reversed the effect of CCh on the adaptation index in dendritic recordings (control 0.39±0.07, CCh –0.41±0.10, CCh + CBA 0.08±0.05; F(2,16) = 34.848; p<0.0005; n=9).
source: and dendritic recordings (control 0.39±0.07, CCh –0.41±0.10, CCh + CBA 0.08±0.05; F(2,16) = 34.848; p<0.0005; n=9; Figure 5B4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: 9-phenanthrol reversed the effect of CCh on the adaptation index in somatic recordings (control 0.40±0.03, CCh –0.14±0.06, CCh + 9Ph 0.19±0.06; F(2,14) = 57.640; p<0.0005; n=8).
source: The differences in adaptation index between groups are significant, as demonstrated by repeated measures ANOVA (control 0.40±0.03, CCh –0.14±0.06, CCh + 9Ph 0.19±0.06; F(2,14) = 57.640; p<0.0005; n=8; Figure 5C4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The shift in adaptation index with CCh is largely mediated through activation of TRPM4, rather than TRPC, channels.
source: Taken together, these data with the non-selective TRP channel blocker FFA, the TRPC channel blocker SKF96365, and two different TRPM4 channel antagonists suggest that the shift in adaptation index that we see with CCh is largely mediated through activation of TRPM4, rather than TRPC, channels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined experimental results with multiple pharmacological agents.

claim: Intracellular Xestospongin C (1–2 µM) did not prevent the cholinergic shift in the center of mass of firing.
source: The adaptation index still decreased significantly (t(8) = 10.574, p<0.0005; n=9, as per a paired t-test) from 0.31±0.02 in control conditions to –0.38±0.07 in the presence of CCh (2 µM). This result argues strongly against the hypothesis that the effects of the activation of muscarinic receptors on the shift of the center of mass of firing are mediated by activation of IP3Rs.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The effects of the activation of muscarinic receptors on the shift of the center of mass of firing are not mediated by activation of IP3Rs.
source: This result argues strongly against the hypothesis that the effects of the activation of muscarinic receptors on the shift of the center of mass of firing are mediated by activation of IP3Rs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results with Xestospongin C.

claim: Intracellular ryanodine (40 µM) did not prevent the cholinergic shift in the center of mass of firing (control 0.28±0.05, CCh –0.46±0.07; t(8) = 11.99; p<0.0005; n=9).
source: Upon addition of CCh in the bath, the adaptation index became significantly more negative in all nine neurons recorded with intracellular ryanodine, as per a paired t-test (control 0.28±0.05, CCh –0.46±0.07; t(8) = 11.99; p<0.0005; n=9), suggesting that RyRs also do not play a role in the cholinergic shift of the center of mass of firing.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: RyRs do not play a role in the cholinergic shift of the center of mass of firing.
source: Upon addition of CCh in the bath, the adaptation index became significantly more negative in all nine neurons recorded with intracellular ryanodine, as per a paired t-test (control 0.28±0.05, CCh –0.46±0.07; t(8) = 11.99; p<0.0005; n=9), suggesting that RyRs also do not play a role in the cholinergic shift of the center of mass of firing.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results with ryanodine.

claim: The model replicates the experimentally observed decrease in spike number and frequency on the down-ramp as compared to the up-ramp (adaptation index = 0.28).
source: The control simulation for a 2 s somatic ramp in Figure 7A1 captures the experimentally observed decrease in spike number and frequency on the down-ramp as compared to the up-ramp (adaptation index = 0.28), as well as a slight decrease in spike amplitude, previously shown to be due to a decrease in available NaV channels (Upchurch et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Adding the Ca2+ influx from an unknown source to a nanodomain in order to simulate bath application of CCh replicates the experimentally observed shift in adaptation index, with more spikes occurring on the down-ramp as compared to the up-ramp (adaptation index = –0.29).
source: Adding the Ca2+ influx from an unknown source to a nanodomain in order to simulate bath application of CCh (Figure 7B1) replicates the experimentally observed shift in adaptation index, with more spikes occurring on the down-ramp as compared to the up-ramp (adaptation index = –0.29).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Spike rate adaptation is attributed to reduced persistent NaV current due to increased long-term inactivation.
source: Our previous work (Upchurch et al., 2022) attributed spike rate adaptation to reduced persistent NaV current due to increased long-term inactivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Upchurch et al., 2022).

claim: No spike rate adaption was observed in simulated CCh because the TRPM4 current is about 4-fold larger than the persistent NaV current.
source: Nonetheless, no spike rate adaption was observed in simulated CCh in Figure 7B1 because the TRPM4 current is about 4-fold larger than the persistent NaV current (compare Figure 8D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The additional TRPM4 current more than compensates for the smaller level of injected ramp current.
source: Figure 8F shows that the additional TRPM4 current more than compensates for the smaller level of injected ramp current; as a consequence, the net inward current is comparable on the up-ramp and larger in magnitude during the down-ramp for the simulated CCh case than control.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The additional TRPM4 current causes spiking to persist longer despite higher levels of NaV channel inactivation.
source: This causes spiking to persist longer despite higher levels of NaV channel inactivation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results.

claim: 10 mM BAPTA did not prevent the cholinergic-mediated shift (control 0.82±0.05, CCh –0.12±0.11; t(9) = 8.594; p<0.0005; n=10).
source: As previously noted, the addition of CCh in the bath caused a depolarization that was compensated for by the injecting hyperpolarizing current. Moreover, despite the presence of BAPTA, the adaptation index became significantly smaller in the presence of CCh, as per a paired t-test (control 0.82±0.05, CCh –0.12±0.11; t(9) = 8.594; p<0.0005; n=10; Figure 10A3); therefore, 10 mM BAPTA did not prevent the cholinergic-mediated shift.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: 30 mM BAPTA with 100 nM free [Ca2+]i still allowed CCh to have a significant effect on the adaptation index (control 0.62±0.05, CCh 0.37±0.06; t(7) = 5.069; p=0.001; n=8).
source: With a free [Ca2+]i of 100 nM (see Materials and methods), CCh never produced negative adaptation indices that were seen in previous figures, although the Vm did depolarize and was restored by the injection of tonic hyperpolarizing current. CCh still had a significant effect on the adaptation index, as per a paired t-test (control 0.62±0.05, CCh 0.37±0.06; t(7) = 5.069; p=0.001; n=8; Figure 10B3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: 30 mM BAPTA with 10 nM free [Ca2+]i prevented the cholinergic shift in the center of mass of firing (control 0.73±0.03, CCh 0.76±0.03; t(11) = 0.776; p=0.45; n=12).
source: However, when the free [Ca2+]i was adjusted to 10 nM in the presence of intracellular 30 mM BAPTA (Figure 10C), the adaptation index did not change significantly when CCh was applied in the bath (control 0.73±0.03, CCh 0.76±0.03; t(11) = 0.776; p=0.45; n=12; Figure 10C3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: A concentration of BAPTA higher than 10 mM is required to prevent TRPM4 channel activation.
source: These data demonstrate that a concentration of BAPTA higher than the typical value (10 mM) used to disrupt Ca2+-dependent mechanisms (Harney et al., 2006) is required to prevent TRPM4 channel activation, and that free [Ca2+]i of <100 nM is necessary to disrupt TRPM4 channel activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results with different BAPTA concentrations.

claim: Free [Ca2+]i of <100 nM is necessary to disrupt TRPM4 channel activation.
source: These data demonstrate that a concentration of BAPTA higher than the typical value (10 mM) used to disrupt Ca2+-dependent mechanisms (Harney et al., 2006) is required to prevent TRPM4 channel activation, and that free [Ca2+]i of <100 nM is necessary to disrupt TRPM4 channel activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results with different BAPTA concentrations.

claim: The BAPTA data suggest a close physical relationship between the source of Ca2+ and TRPM4 channels.
source: Together, these data suggest a close physical relationship between the source of Ca2+ and TRPM4 channels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results with BAPTA.

source: (4) multicompartmental modeling suggests a close physical relationship between the source of Ca2+ increase and the TRPM4 channels

claim: The major cholinergic input to the hippocampus is from the medial septum and diagonal band of Broca.

claim: Pyramidal neurons express G-protein-coupled metabotropic muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChRs).
source: Pyramidal neurons express G-protein-coupled metabotropic muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChRs; Levey et al., 1995), more so than they do ionotropic (nicotinic) receptors, which are primarily on interneurons in this region (Dani and Bertrand, 2007).

claim: M1 mAChRs are found on both dendritic shafts and spines of CA1 pyramidal neurons.

claim: Elevated acetylcholine in the hippocampal formation is thought to favor memory encoding.

claim: The shift is not blocked by ryanodine receptor antagonists.
source: This shift is blocked by antagonists specific for TRPM4 channels or by intracellular Ca2+ buffering, but not by IP3 or ryanodine receptor antagonists.

claim: TRPM4 channels have a micromolar half-activation concentration of Ca2+.
source: The TRPM4 channels have a micromolar half-activation concentration of Ca2+ (Nilius et al., 2004), which implies that a restricted Ca2+ nanodomain near the channel mouth is required to elicit substantial opening of TRPM4 channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nilius et al., 2004.

claim: A restricted Ca2+ nanodomain near the channel mouth is required to elicit substantial opening of TRPM4 channels.
source: The TRPM4 channels have a micromolar half-activation concentration of Ca2+ (Nilius et al., 2004), which implies that a restricted Ca2+ nanodomain near the channel mouth is required to elicit substantial opening of TRPM4 channels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known Ca2+ affinity of TRPM4 channels.

claim: Whatever the Ca2+ source that activates the TRPM4 channels, it is likely co-localized with them.
source: Thus, whatever the Ca2+ source that activates the TRPM4 channels, it is likely co-localized with them.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the requirement for a nanodomain.

claim: Carbachol tends to shift the center of mass of firing to later in the ramp in the case of a synaptically driven depolarization.
source: These results show that carbachol tends to shift the center of mass of firing to later in the ramp in the case of a synaptically driven depolarization as well as in response to a ramp of injected current.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with synaptic stimulation shown in Figure 2.

claim: The average amplitude of the first EPSP in control (8.83±0.82 mV) was significantly larger than the average first EPSP in CCh (6.81±0.52 mV; t(10) = 4.127; p=0.002; n=11).
source: This shift was partly due to a decrease in the amplitude of the EPSPs (Figure 2D); the average amplitude of the first EPSP in control (8.83±0.82 mV) was significantly larger than the average first EPSP in CCh (6.81±0.52 mV; t(10) = 4.127; p=0.002; n=11).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The decay of the EPSPs appeared to slow down later in the ramp in the presence of CCh.
source: In addition, the decay of the EPSPs appeared to slow down later in the ramp in the presence of CCh (compare EPSPs indicated by diamonds in the two conditions), resulting in an increase in temporal summation and excitability.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Carbachol is not susceptible to hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase.
source: Carbachol is often used to more easily study cholinergic signaling in biological tissues, because it is not susceptible to hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase, which is preserved and active in hippocampal slices (Avignone and Cherubini, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Avignone and Cherubini, 1999 and is established knowledge.

claim: Acetylcholinesterase is preserved and active in hippocampal slices.
source: Carbachol is often used to more easily study cholinergic signaling in biological tissues, because it is not susceptible to hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase, which is preserved and active in hippocampal slices (Avignone and Cherubini, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Avignone and Cherubini, 1999.

claim: Acetylcholine caused a depolarization of the Vm in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Acetylcholine caused a depolarization of the Vm in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations reported in the manuscript.

claim: The actual concentration of ACh in the slices is likely lower than the applied one due to degradation via acetylcholinesterase.
source: Due to likely degradation via acetylcholinesterase, we speculate that the actual concentration in the slices is lower than the applied one.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation informed by knowledge of acetylcholinesterase activity.

claim: Fluctuations in ACh levels could have implications for the firing of a place cell within its place field.
source: Fluctuations in ACh levels could therefore have implications for the firing of a place cell within its place field.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation informed by the experimental results.

claim: Place fields expand and the center of mass shifts backward with respect to the direction of travel on continuous tracks over several laps during each recording session.
source: In vivo recordings in rats demonstrated that place fields expand and the center of mass shifts backward with respect to the direction of travel on continuous tracks over several laps during each recording session (Mehta et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mehta et al., 2000.

claim: NMDA blockers occlude the backwards shift of the place field.
source: NMDA blockers were subsequently shown to occlude the backwards shift of the place field (Ekstrom et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ekstrom et al., 2001.

claim: An NMDA agonist partially restored the backwards shift in aged rats.
source: and an NMDA agonist partially restored it in aged rats (Burke et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Burke et al., 2008.

claim: Calcium imaging in mice running on a treadmill in a virtual environment showed an abrupt backward shift in place cell firing during the first exposure to a novel environment.
source: Calcium imaging in mice running on a treadmill in a virtual environment showed an abrupt backward shift in place cell firing (relative to where the first episode of place field firing occurred) during the first exposure to a novel environment (Priestley et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Priestley et al., 2022.

claim: Much smaller backward shifts in place fields in novel environments leveled off as the animals became more familiar with the environment during subsequent exposures.
source: as well as much smaller backward shifts in place fields in novel environments that leveled off as the animals became more familiar with the environment during subsequent exposures (Dong et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dong et al., 2021.

claim: Forward shifting of the center of mass of place field firing occurred, shifting toward prospective goal locations in the continuous T-maze alternation task as a reward was approached.
source: Forward shifting of the center of mass of place field firing occurred, shifting toward prospective goal locations in the continuous T-maze alternation task as a reward was approached (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2006.

claim: The center of mass of CA1 place fields in laps 2–4 were forward shifted compared to the first lap, for cells that already had a place field on the first lap.
source: In a study that did not involve reward, but only exploration of a novel virtual linear maze (Dong et al., 2021), the center of mass of CA1 place fields in laps 2–4 were forward shifted compared to the first lap, for cells that already had a place field on the first lap (a lap required approximately 25 s).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dong et al., 2021.

claim: Laps 5 and beyond were backward shifted compared to the immediately preceding lap.
source: Laps 5 and beyond were backward shifted compared to the immediately preceding lap, so averaging over all runs, the place field was shifted backwards.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dong et al., 2021.

claim: Increasing levels of ACh could lead to forward shifts in place field center of mass.
source: Our results suggest that increasing levels of ACh could lead to forward shifts in place field center of mass whereas decreasing levels of ACh could contribute to backwards shifts.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation informed by the experimental results.

claim: Decreasing levels of ACh could contribute to backwards shifts in place field center of mass.
source: Our results suggest that increasing levels of ACh could lead to forward shifts in place field center of mass whereas decreasing levels of ACh could contribute to backwards shifts.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation informed by the experimental results.

claim: The rapid modulation of ion channels by removal of cholinergic tone could provide a possible mechanism for the rapid shifting of place cell firing in a novel versus familiar environment.
source: The rapid modulation of ion channels by removal of cholinergic tone could therefore provide a possible mechanism for the rapid shifting of place cell firing in a novel versus familiar environment, perhaps complementary to Hebbian plasticity that develops over time.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation informed by the experimental results.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of medial septum cholinergic afferents to CA1 during runs through a place field in a novel environment should partially occlude backwards shifts in place field center on subsequent runs.
source: If our hypothesis is correct, optogenetic silencing of medial septum cholinergic afferents to CA1 during runs through a place field in a novel environment should partially occlude backwards shifts in place field center on subsequent runs that are due to diminished ACh in a familiar environment.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about future experiments.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of medial septum cholinergic afferents during runs in a familiar environment should induce forward shifts in place field centers.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of the same afferents during runs in a familiar environment should induce forward shifts in place field centers.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about future experiments.

claim: Neuromodulation of intrinsic properties by ACh provide an additional level of modulatory control in parallel with synaptic plasticity mechanisms, contributing to rapid place field shifts.
source: We propose that neuromodulation of intrinsic properties by ACh, and potentially other neuromodulators like dopamine, provide an additional level of modulatory control in parallel with synaptic plasticity mechanisms, contributing to rapid place field shifts.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation informed by the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Muscarinic activation of a Ca2+-dependent nonselective cation current in rat CA1 pyramidal neurons has been known for nearly three decades.
source: Muscarinic activation of a Ca2+-dependent nonselective cation current in rat CA1 pyramidal neurons has been known for nearly three decades (Colino and Halliwell, 1993; Fraser and MacVicar, 1996; Dasari et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Colino and Halliwell, 1993; Fraser and MacVicar, 1996; and Dasari et al., 2017.

claim: In mouse CA1 neurons, muscarinic stimulation not only inhibits background potassium currents but also activates a nonselective cation current.
source: A previous study Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013 found that in mouse CA1 neurons as well, muscarinic stimulation not only inhibits background potassium currents but also activates a nonselective cation current.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013.

claim: Muscarinic stimulation converted CA1 pyramidal neurons into pacemakers with the application of 5–25 μM acetylcholine, 5–25 μM carbachol, or 5–10 μM oxotremorine-M.
source: They found that the latter effect was dominant and in fact converted CA1 pyramidal neurons into pacemakers with the application of 5–25 μM acetylcholine, 5–25 μM carbachol, or 5–10 μM oxotremorine-M.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013.

claim: The unidentified channel in Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013 could be the TRPM4 channel.
source: They suggested TRPC channels might mediate this current but were unable to positively identify the source of the nonselective cation current. Based on our results, this unidentified channel could be the TRPM4 channel.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation informed by the experimental results.

claim: The activation of TRPM4 channels contribute an additional inward current that activates and deactivates slowly upon depolarization.
source: Our model shows that the activation of TRPM4 channels contribute an additional inward current that activates and deactivates slowly upon depolarization.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results.

claim: The inward TRPM4 current with its slow kinetics is likely to cause an increased decay time of the EPSPs.
source: In the case of synaptically driven depolarizations (Figure 2), this inward current, with its slow kinetics (see Figures 8 and 9) is likely to cause an increased decay time of the EPSPs (see Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the modeling and experimental results.

claim: The increased decay time of EPSPs has likely implications for synaptic integration by CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: This aspect has likely implications for synaptic integration by these neurons, as shown by the observation of an impairment of LTP in TRPM4 knockout mice (Menigoz et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on inference supported by citation to Menigoz et al., 2016.

claim: TRPC channels have been implicated in downstream effects associated with Gq-coupled signaling.
source: The TRPC subfamily has been implicated as being responsible for ICAN in some neurons and is thought to be activated by elements downstream of muscarinic acetylcholine receptor activation (Putney, 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Putney, 2005.

claim: Cholinergic stimulation of Gq/11-coupled mAChRs results in phospholipase C hydrolysis of PIP2 into IP3 and DAG.
source: Cholinergic stimulation of Gq/11-coupled mAChRs results in phospholipase C hydrolysis of membrane constituent phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) into inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of signaling pathways.

claim: IP3 stimulates IP3R associated Ca2+ release from the endoplasmic reticulum, regulating TRPC channel activity via calmodulin.
source: IP3 stimulates IP3 receptor (IP3R) associated Ca2+ release from the endoplasmic reticulum, regulating TRPC channel activity via calmodulin (Zhu, 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhu, 2005.

claim: DAG activates TRPC channels directly.
source: while DAG activates TRPC channels directly (Hofmann et al., 1999; Mederos Y Schnitzler et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hofmann et al., 1999 and Mederos Y Schnitzler et al., 2018.

claim: TRPM4 channels have likewise been implicated in downstream effects associated with Gq-coupled signaling.
source: TRPM4 channels have likewise been implicated in downstream effects associated with Gq-coupled signaling (Launay et al., 2002; Dutta Banik et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Launay et al., 2002 and Dutta Banik et al., 2018.

claim: TRPM4 channels are activated by Ca2+ binding to the cytoplasmic side combined with depolarization.
source: TRPM4 channels are activated by Ca2+ binding to the cytoplasmic side combined with depolarization (Nilius et al., 2003; Autzen et al., 2018), but these channels are impermeable to Ca2+.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nilius et al., 2003 and Autzen et al., 2018.

claim: TRPM4 channels are impermeable to Ca2+.
source: TRPM4 channels are activated by Ca2+ binding to the cytoplasmic side combined with depolarization (Nilius et al., 2003; Autzen et al., 2018), but these channels are impermeable to Ca2+.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nilius et al., 2003 and Autzen et al., 2018.

claim: TRPM4 channels facilitate a rise in [Ca2+]i indirectly, by depolarizing the membrane potential and therefore activating voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: Instead, TRPM4 channels facilitate a rise in [Ca2+]i indirectly, by depolarizing the membrane potential (Launay et al., 2002) and therefore activating voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Launay et al., 2002 and Li et al., 2021.

claim: Cationic current through TRPM4 channels and the resulting [Ca2+]i elevation has been implicated in bursting, persistent firing, and oscillatory activity in some neurons.
source: Cationic current through these channels and the resulting [Ca2+]i elevation has been implicated in bursting, persistent firing, and oscillatory activity in some neurons (Lin et al., 2017; O'Malley et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2017; O'Malley et al., 2020; and Li et al., 2021.

claim: In HEK cells transfected with cDNA encoding TRPM4 channels, and in cardiac myocytes, activation of TRPM4 channels is secondary to IP3 receptor activation.
source: In HEK cells transfected with cDNA encoding TRPM4 channels, and in cardiac myocytes, activation of TRPM4 channels is secondary to IP3 receptor activation (Launay et al., 2002; Gonzales et al., 2010; Gonzales and Earley, 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Launay et al., 2002; Gonzales et al., 2010; and Gonzales and Earley, 2012.

claim: In situ proximity ligation assay was used to demonstrate co-localization of TRPM4 channels and IP3Rs in human detrusor smooth muscle cells.
source: Furthermore, in situ proximity ligation assay was used to demonstrate co-localization of TRPM4 channels and IP3Rs in human detrusor smooth muscle cells (Provence et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Provence et al., 2017.

claim: In neurons of the preBötzinger nucleus TRPM4 channels are recruited by metabotropic glutamate receptors to generate robust inspiratory drive potentials through IP3R activation.
source: In addition, in neurons of the preBötzinger nucleus TRPM4 channels are recruited by metabotropic glutamate receptors to generate robust inspiratory drive potentials through IP3R activation (Pace et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pace et al., 2007.

claim: Ca2+ release from the ER was not involved in the cholinergic shift of the center of mass of firing.
source: Surprisingly, we found that Ca2+ release from the ER was not involved in the cholinergic shift of the center of mass of firing, since neither the IP3R antagonist Xestospongin C (1–2 µM) nor the RyR antagonist ryanodine (40 µM) prevented the effects of carbachol.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with IP3R and RyR antagonists.

claim: TRPM4 channels act as coincidence detectors, requiring both muscarinic receptor activation and depolarization-induced Ca2+ influx during the ramp to be activated.
source: Therefore, although the mechanisms that produce the micromolar [Ca2+] increases needed for TRPM4 channel activation are unknown, our results point to these channels acting as coincidence detectors, requiring both muscarinic receptor activation and depolarization-induced Ca2+ influx during the ramp to be activated.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Both CBA and 9-phenanthrol have been shown to decrease the Ito1 potassium current in cardiac cells.
source: In cardiac cells, both CBA and 9-phenanthrol have been shown to decrease the Ito1 potassium current, attributed to Kv4.3 (Veress et al., 2018; Dienes et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Veress et al., 2018 and Dienes et al., 2021.

claim: Both CBA and 9-phenanthrol have been shown to decrease a late sodium current in cardiac cells.
source: and a late sodium current (Hou et al., 2018; Dienes et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hou et al., 2018 and Dienes et al., 2021.

claim: Kv4.3 is likely more important in interneurons than in pyramidal cells in the CA1 area.
source: Kv4.3 is likely more important in interneurons than in pyramidal cells in the CA1 area (Martina et al., 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Martina et al., 1998.

claim: Neither Ito1 nor late sodium current are affected by FFA at the concentration used in this study.
source: and neither of the two currents are affected by FFA at the concentration we used here (Guinamard et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Guinamard et al., 2013.

claim: The convergent effects of FFA, CBA and 9-phenanthrol implicate TRPM4 channels as the most probable effector of the CCh-mediated modulation of the center of mass of firing.
source: The convergent effects of these three distinct drugs implicate TRPM4 channels as the most probable effector of the CCh-mediated modulation of the center of mass of firing.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined pharmacological results.

claim: A similar pharmacological approach was used to implicate TRPM4 channel activation in subthreshold oscillations underlying pacemaker firing of chemosensory neurons in the retrotrapezoid nucleus.
source: A similar pharmacological approach was used to implicate TRPM4 channel activation in subthreshold oscillations underlying pacemaker firing of chemosensory neurons in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2021.

claim: ACh binding to muscarinic receptors results in neuromodulation of neuronal excitability and presynaptic release probability in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: In CA1 pyramidal neurons, ACh binding to muscarinic receptors results in neuromodulation of neuronal excitability and presynaptic release probability.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of cholinergic signaling.

claim: Muscarinic receptors suppress several K+ currents in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Muscarinic receptors are known to suppress several K+ currents in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Halliwell and Adams, 1982; Hoffman and Johnston, 1998; Buchanan et al., 2010; Giessel and Sabatini, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Halliwell and Adams, 1982; Hoffman and Johnston, 1998; Buchanan et al., 2010; and Giessel and Sabatini, 2010.

claim: The effects of ACh on SK, M-type currents and ICAN are mediated by M1 (Gq-coupled) receptors.
source: The effects of ACh on SK, M-type currents and ICAN are mediated by M1 (Gq-coupled) receptors (Dasari and Gulledge, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dasari and Gulledge, 2011.

claim: Synaptic depression of Schaffer collateral inputs to CA1 is mediated by M4 (Gi-coupled) receptors.
source: Synaptic depression of Schaffer collateral inputs to CA1 is mediated by M4 (Gi-coupled) receptors (Dasari and Gulledge, 2011) located on presynaptic glutamatergic terminals
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dasari and Gulledge, 2011.

claim: Synaptic depression of temporoammonic pathway glutamatergic inputs to CA1 is mediated by M3 (Gq-coupled) receptors.
source: and synaptic depression of temporoammonic pathway glutamatergic inputs to CA1 is mediated by M3 (Gq-coupled) receptors (Palacios-Filardo et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Palacios-Filardo et al., 2021.

claim: Decreased release from Schaffer collateral was indicated by the smaller amplitude EPSPs in the presence of CCh.
source: When we used a synaptically driven depolarization (Figure 2), decreased release from Schaffer collateral was indicated by the smaller amplitude EPSPs in the presence of CCh.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A combination of pre- and postsynaptic effects of cholinergic agonists can contribute to the shift in center of mass of firing.
source: In these experiments, as in the current injection protocols, the center of mass of firing occurred earlier in the ramp in control and shifted to later in the ramp in the presence of CCh, suggesting that a combination of pre- and postsynaptic effects of cholinergic agonists can contribute to the shift.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The cholinergic down-regulation of Schaffer collateral afferents justifies the use of smaller depolarizing current injection ramps in the presence of carbachol.
source: Moreover, the cholinergic down-regulation of these afferents justifies the use of smaller depolarizing current injection ramps in our recordings in the presence of carbachol, because less current injection is required to produce the same output frequencies due to enhanced intrinsic excitability in carbachol.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: In a model of place field formation, if a neuron randomly fires within a place field, its inputs from the currently active grid cells are strengthened and the input from those grid cells onto silent cells are weakened.
source: In a model of place field formation (Savelli and Knierim, 2010), if a neuron randomly fires within a place field (Bittner et al., 2015), its inputs from the currently active grid cells are strengthened and the input from those grid cells onto silent cells are weakened.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Savelli and Knierim, 2010 and Bittner et al., 2015.

claim: All hippocampal cholinergic terminals form synapses.
source: Recently, this view has been challenged by the finding that all hippocampal cholinergic terminals form synapses (Takács et al., 2018), and vesicles dock only at synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takács et al., 2018.

claim: Vesicles dock only at synapses in hippocampal cholinergic terminals.
source: Recently, this view has been challenged by the finding that all hippocampal cholinergic terminals form synapses (Takács et al., 2018), and vesicles dock only at synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takács et al., 2018.

claim: Selective synaptic ACh inputs may underlie the formation of place fields in a novel environment.
source: Since cholinergic neuromodulation of TRPM4 channels greatly increases excitability in CA1 pyramidal cells, selective synaptic ACh inputs may underlie the formation of place fields in a novel environment.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation informed by the experimental results.

claim: ACh terminals co-released GABA in separate vesicles.
source: Moreover, Takács et al., 2018 found that the ACh terminals co-released GABA in separate vesicles, and that ACh acting on M2 (Gi-coupled) autoreceptors on cholinergic terminals inhibited the release of both ACh and GABA.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takács et al., 2018.

claim: ACh acting on M2 (Gi-coupled) autoreceptors on cholinergic terminals inhibited the release of both ACh and GABA.
source: Moreover, Takács et al., 2018 found that the ACh terminals co-released GABA in separate vesicles, and that ACh acting on M2 (Gi-coupled) autoreceptors on cholinergic terminals inhibited the release of both ACh and GABA.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takács et al., 2018.

claim: Acetylcholine acting at muscarinic receptors has been hypothesized to be a global novelty signal in the dentate gyrus.
source: Acetylcholine acting at muscarinic receptors has been hypothesized to be a global novelty signal in the dentate gyrus (Gómez-Ocádiz et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gómez-Ocádiz et al., 2022.

claim: Acetylcholine acting at muscarinic receptors has been hypothesized to be a global novelty signal in the dorsal hippocampus.
source: dorsal hippocampus (Huff et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Huff et al., 2022.

claim: Acetylcholine acting at muscarinic receptors has been hypothesized to be a global novelty signal in the parahippocampal gyrus.
source: and the parahippocampal gyrus (Frank and Kafkas, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Frank and Kafkas, 2021.

claim: A novel unconditioned stimulus caused a large increase in ACh extracellular levels in the hippocampus, but little locomotion.
source: A novel unconditioned stimulus caused a large increase in ACh extracellular levels in the hippocampus, but little locomotion (Acquas et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Acquas et al., 1996.

claim: Hippocampal ACh release in an animal placed in a novel environment has two components, one related to novelty, that disappears in a familiar environment, and one related to motor activity, associated with increased exploration.
source: On the other hand, hippocampal ACh release in an animal placed in a novel environment has two components, one related to novelty, that disappears in a familiar environment (Thiel et al., 1998), and one related to motor activity, associated with increased exploration (Giovannini et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thiel et al., 1998 and Giovannini et al., 2001.

claim: Part of the population activity in medial septal cholinergic neurons is correlated with the logarithm of running speed.
source: Indeed, a recent fiber photometric study showed that part of the population activity in medial septal cholinergic neurons is correlated with the logarithm of running speed (Kopsick et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kopsick et al., 2022.
